utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution is continuing examination-in-chief. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, just before I do, Ms. Reidy looked into the question of authenticity of exhibits yesterday and -- yesterday afternoon, and I think is in a position to inform the Chamber of what precisely the Defence have agreed and haven't agreed, and possibly lay to rest any misgivings about authenticity that might be troubling the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Reidy?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll just be one minute. Yesterday, Mr. Pantelic referred to correspondence inter partes concerning authenticity. This was a document the Defence sent us on the 15th of September, 2001, indicating those which they have no objection to on admissibility or authenticity, the majority of them, and a number where they had no objection to admissibility but had objections to the authenticity of it and they requested that they -- that we produce the original documents for inspection, and if we could provide an additional description of when, where, and by whom the above-specified documents were seized in order to resolve the issue of authenticity. All of that was complied with. I'm afraid I can't tell you the exact date of the response because my cover note is missing from the file. Within a matter of days, I supplied to all the Defence counsel a copy of the signed receipt of, I believe it was 258 -- or 158 documents, that we received with a signed receipt from Mirko Lukic, who was President of the Municipal Assembly of the municipality of Bosanski Samac on the 11th of June, 1998. It explains clearly where the documents came from, who they given to, where they were taken from. It was given to each Defence counsel. I consulted with them this morning. They acknowledge having received it. Mr. Pantelic acknowledges having received this back in September. It seems to me that he has -- since then, we heard nothing back from him, having provided everything they wanted on the matter of authenticity and where we got the documents from. And if he still has objections, he has given us no indications what steps since September he has taken to further raise with us any issues of authenticity. But following that correspondence back in September, the only outstanding matter, in fact, with Variant A/B document, which has been dealt with, and one of the documents that was admitted in that process of verification of the Variant A/B document. So as far as the Prosecution is concerned, we had correspondence with the parties over this. We provided them with all the information, and it just seems that Mr. Pantelic has let this slip his mind since September that we provided the information about where and from whom, et cetera, these documents came from. And he certainly never came back to the Prosecution on any document beyond Variant A/Variant B since September last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, it's not so big matter to have the time for discussing. I don't have in my record -- just to correct Ms. Reidy, I don't have this letter in my archive so I have to check with my friends. They will be probably very kind to check their records. And in the break, we shall resolve the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's a matter you can resolve, find out from your documents and deal with it with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just for the record, I didn't receive that letter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We continue, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours. Can the witness be shown Exhibit P36? May I just see it briefly before it's presented to the witness? That's the one. Thank you. Examined by Mr. Di Fazio: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, just quickly have a look at that document and acquaint yourself with its general nature. I won't be long on the document, Mr. Todorovic. If you could just skim through it and essentially get an idea of its nature, what it's generally about, okay? First of all, the signature, can you tell us again, and I appreciate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to my learned colleague. If the B/C/S could be placed on the ELMO for our clients, because they don't know what the document is that we are talking about because the English version is on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps the Prosecution has always to make sure you have a photocopy of the B/C/S, the rest of the document, so that can be on the ELMO. MR. DI FAZIO: For the sake of convenience, I've got my own B/C/S version here -- I have a blank version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If you have a clean copy, yes, put it on the ELMO, please. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now to return to my question, just the signature again, Mr. Todorovic. I know you're not a handwriting expert and you're not being asked to comment as a handwriting expert, but can you give --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise but I have a document on one -- I have one document and there is another document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We have B/C/S version, Your Honours, if that may be of assistance, to speed up things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just answer that one question and then I'll finish with the document. You recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour, again. Yesterday, my learned friend from the Prosecution passed through all these questions. This witness said he stands beside these documents. I really don't see why we have to go this repetitive -- he answered a number of questions about this very document, Your Honour. And he said, "I stand beside this document, I -- my lawyer was not in my office. I called another lawyer."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, he explained. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't intend to dwell on the document. That was the only matter I wanted to raise and I'll leave it alone. The document can be finished with. Would Your Honours just bear with me for one moment? Thank you. If Your Honours please, I want to produce a document. Defence counsel will know of it as C21.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Todorovic, I don't want to dwell too long on this particular document. Can you just quickly have a look at it and acquaint yourself with its general nature? And I just want to take you to certain portions of the document. Who is the apparent author of the document? You'll see that at the end.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, in the heading, it says, "The command of the 17th Corps." And it was delivered to the 2nd Military District headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is Savo Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Savo Jankovic was the commander of the Tuzla Corps in April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the Tuzla Corps based -- sorry, yeah, where was it based, what area? Was it in Tuzla or did it cover a much wider area?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the Tuzla Corps, as far as I know, had its seat in Tuzla but it covered a wider area, and at that time, the 17th Tactical Group also was part of this corps, that is to say, the municipality of Bosanski Samac area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Tuzla Corps later change its name?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Tuzla Corps later changed its name to the East Bosnia Corps. It only changed its name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you go to paragraph 4 of the letter, or the report, there is a reference to "TO units disarming paramilitary groups and armed civilians." You touched upon this topic yesterday but, again, what is the meaning of TO units there, as far as you can tell?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a military expert, but as far as I know, the Territorial Defence consisted of these four detachments that were part of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, it refers to numbers of losses and wounded men that the Serb forces suffered. They refer to two men from Tactical Group 17 troops having been lightly wounded. Doing the best you can - I know it's a long time ago - but can you give us any idea if that fits in with your memory of the sort of losses suffered by the 17th Tactical Group in those initial days?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of wounding of one member of the 17th Tactical Group but it's possible that there might have been another man wounded, but I don't have any concrete information on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This is dated the 19th of April, 1992, two days after events started in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those two days, presumably, then the unit, the 4th Detachment, did not suffer any significant losses?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, these first few days, the 4th Detachment did not suffer any losses, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I produce the document, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be P80/ter, Your Honours, for the B/C/S version and P80 for the English version. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Todorovic, I want to move now to another aspect of events soon after the 16th and 17th, that is, the arrests. First of all, there is little doubt in this case that there were significant numbers of arrests that occurred in Bosanski Samac. That's not in issue. In the days and weeks and months following the 16th and 17th of April, after people had been arrested and imprisoned, who was overall in charge, to whom did the overall responsibility lie, for the health and protection of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The highest responsibility for the protection of the detainees lay with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff have any collective responsibility for the detainees and the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I'm competent to decide on this. I think that's something that the Trial Chamber should decide on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you inform, either formally or informally, in writing or not in writing, other members of the Crisis Staff of the situation generally in relation to detainees?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My responsibility as the police chief was to verbally, orally, inform the Crisis Staff about the political and security situation within the municipality of Bosanski Samac from time to time, and this included informing them about prisons and the people that were detained. But I did not inform them about all the details, but generally speaking, yes, and I was doing this verbally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to know who conducted the arrests in the days and weeks and months following the 16th and 17th of April. Presumably, it was members of the police, but did other groups also participate in the arrests, such as the 4th Detachment and the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first night, and also the first and the second day, the arrests and the detentions of the armed Muslim-Croat formations were done by the members of the 4th Detachment along with the police, but also by members of other detachments, if somewhere on the grounds they apprehended a member of the Croat-Muslim units, and this is because the command of the 14th Tactical Group was quite far from Samac. Later, the arrests were done by the members of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did numbers in the SUP quickly reach a point where the place was overflowing and accommodation had to be found in the TO building as well?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very quickly the rooms became too small, because they were not built for a larger number of people. Then we placed the rest of the detainees into the rooms of the Territorial Defence building, which is across the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you in the question before whether the paramilitaries also participated in the arrests because, of course, they were going around the town on the night of the 16th and 17th. Can you tell us if they brought in people themselves?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They also did that personally.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpretation correction: On page 8, line 24, it should say "17th Tactical Group," not "14th."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I was about to ask the Prosecution about that, actually. So it should be 17th Tactical Group, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes I'm grateful to the interpreters for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And members of the 4th Detachment, can you give us any idea of what sort of numbers of people they brought in on the first two or three days?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first two or three days, they brought in about 20 or 30 people, for sure, but I cannot recall the exact number because it was very chaotic and everybody who had arms - I'm referring to the Serbs - brought a neighbour in and said, "This person has a sniper or a rifle." And then they would bring them to the station. On the first day, they were cleansing, so to speak, half of the town. When I say "they," I mean the special units members. And the second portion of the town was cleaned up by the 4th Detachment members. When I say "cleaned or cleansed," I'm referring to them going from house to house and searching the apartments and houses for weapons. And then if they would find weapons somewhere, they would bring these weapons to the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever form an impression as to what was required before a member of the paramilitary forces or the 4th Detachment would arrest a person, detain them? Was much required? Did they have to have definite proof of ownership of military weapons or membership of a paramilitary formation? Or were people arrested --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think that is loaded, Mr. Di Fazio, and it does contain some important points, I think. Can you just break it down? MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What criteria was being used by members of the paramilitary forces or the 4th Detachment in order to arrest someone? What did someone have to do to be arrested?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- those were arrested who had weapons, illegal weapons, or explosives with them, or it was known as a fact that they prepared an armed insurgence or that they participated in the procurement of illegal weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a paramilitary went to the home of someone in Bosanski Samac and arrested that person, would he have had -- that particular paramilitary have had any idea of the background of the person, their participation in any sort of paramilitary formation, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that this is calling for speculation. If he had any knowledge, did he have? This is another person. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if the witness can answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic, I think, is right, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll withdraw it and pose this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any briefing given to the paramilitaries, members of the 4th Detachment or police, as to the names of the people they should arrest?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of them got some instructions. We had certain knowledge about these things. We even seized a folder and some documents, and names of people who were armed were in those documents. In one folder, we found a list and military organisation of the Party of Democratic Action, and we could see according to sections, names and phone numbers of people that were members of that section. If a member of the 4th Detachment or a policeman or a townsperson were to tell a special units member about -- to arrest certain people because the special units member is not from Samac so they wouldn't know, then the special units member would go and arrest that person, and also if in their apartment they would find a radio station or a rifle or some other kind of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were people ever arrested when they weren't in possession of a rifle or ammunition or any sort of military equipment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour. It seems to us that this witness said, in line 21 of page 11, after "ammunition," we think that he said also "explosives." Maybe our learned friend from Prosecution can clarify that. Maybe we are mistaken, I don't know. But it seems to us that he mentioned a word "explosives" also, which might be of importance for this testimony. Maybe it's a matter of translation or maybe they didn't catch the word or something. So...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think Mr. Di Fazio can clear that with the witness. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you also mention the word "explosives" in your previous answer?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. I mentioned the word "explosives."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the phenomenon of these arrests continue throughout the ensuing months or did the pace of arrests slow down after the first few days?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the first few days, the intensity diminished, but arrests did occur if some additional information was gained through investigations of the arrested or if the police found additional written documents or acquired new insight in the cases. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, did you provide a series of interviews to officers of the OTP in early last year, early year 2001?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you accompanied on that occasion by your lawyer, Mr. Dejan Brasic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On a few occasions, Mr. Brasic was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in particular, were you interviewed on the 18th of January, 2001?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to put to you something that you said, and ask you to comment upon it. You were being asked questions by a woman called Nancy Paterson, who was the then-Prosecutor in this case. And she asked you this question, and you provided this answer. Question: And who issued the orders to go around and arrest these people?"

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise again, Your Honour. Could Mr. Di Fazio just give us a short reference, which page, so that we can follow? It's a bundle of documents. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's more than 2.000 pages. Thank you in advance. MR. DI FAZIO: I do apologise to my learned friends. I should have mentioned that. It's the 18th of January - I'm looking at the English version - and it's page 30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Question from Nancy Paterson: "And who issued the orders to go around and arrest these people? Did you order it? Did the Crisis Staff order it?" You answered: "In those first days, arrests happened more or less spontaneously. Men who were in the field brought in people in whose apartments they found radio transmitters or weapons or people who they suspected to be snipers. There was no firm criteria or clear order in that respect." When you said there was no firm criteria, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I meant that there was no precise criteria, nor was there a special list of people who had to be arrested. There was no specific list of persons drafted before the 17th, but on the basis of the investigations that we carried out and the documentation, the documents we also got our hands on concerning the Croatian and the Muslim elements in the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the days and weeks following the 17th of April, did the Crisis Staff ever participate in the decision to arrest people or classes of people?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff de facto supported such an activity but I don't remember any strict written instruction but the position was that the Croats and Muslims with arms, who were preparing armed insurgences were to be questioned, interrogated and that an investigation was to be carried out against them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I mean -- sorry, what I need to know is, when you say that Croats and Muslims with arms who were preparing armed insurgencies were to be questioned, interrogated and investigated, did the Crisis Staff actually participate in that decision, to question, interrogate, arrest them and so on?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Crisis Staff in fact approved this undertaking, this action, which was underway from the first day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to refer to another interview you gave. Again, it was in fact at the very end of the year 2000. It was, in fact, your first interview, and again, you were accompanied by your lawyer, and on this particular occasion, you were being asked questions by an investigator. MR. DI FAZIO: And the date of the interview, if Your Honours please, is the 6th of November, and for the benefit of my learned friends, I'm referring to the English transcript, page 55 and 56.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to put a series of questions and answers and see if you agree with the content of what you said. Mr. Selsky, who was the interviewer asked you, "Were civilians detained? Civilians other than opposition soldiers, were civilians detained?" You answered, "There were such cases, yes." Question: "Where did you receive your orders on who to detain and for how long?" And you answered, "Orders came from the Crisis Staff and also from investigators, investigators who worked in the criminal investigation service. When they would come across some information about someone, somebody's involvement in armed insurgence, They would act on them." That's what you told the investigators. Do you agree with that position?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Who had the power to release detained persons?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as the bigger groups were concerned, the right to release them, that was in the hands of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, do you think we could find out what Mr. Todorovic means by "bigger groups," which is on line 18? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard Her Honour's question. You referred to bigger groups. Are you there referring to classes of people, types of people, or something else? Can you tell us what you meant when you said "bigger groups"?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- when saying, speaking of a bigger group of detainees, I'm thinking of detainees who, from detention, went into the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'll see if I can get some further details about that from you. Can you recall any specific examples of when the Crisis Staff or Crisis Staff members made a decision as to whether or not someone should be kept in custody or released?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember individual decisions concerning a single person, but I remember that, at the beginning, there was the general position that, in order to save Serbs who were detained in Odzak, that an agreement was given that a group of detained Croats and Muslims could be exchanged for the detained Serbs in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll get to that issue of exchanges later. Perhaps I'll approach it this way. Do you know a gentleman named Sulejman Tihic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he -- he was arrested, I think, fairly early on after the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you actively looking for him early on, that is around the 17th of April, you and the police force, searching for him?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the first day, the members of the police and the others were looking for him, but he was not to be found at his address. We were looking for him because he was the main person involved in procuring -- in illegal procurements of weapons for the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any information as to his whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did receive some information, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who provided you with that information?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this information was passed on to me by Mr. Blagoje Simic because, prior to that, he talked to him or to Mr. Pisarevic over the phone, but he told me that he was to be found in Pisarevic's apartment, that Mr. Pisarevic was hiding him in his own apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you receive instructions to arrest him?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't receive - how to put it - a precise instruction, "Go and arrest him," but I did receive the information, "You're looking for him throughout the town but he is to be found in Mr. Pisarevic's apartment."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you remember when you received that information from Mr. Blagoje Simic? Was it on the 17th or the 18th? Or if you can't remember, say so.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was it the 17th or the 17th or 18th, but it -- at the latest, on the 19th. That information was received on one of these days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. I just want to put another passage to you again from the interviews that were conducted with you and see what you say about it. This is an interview that was conducted with you on the 18th of January, 2001. Again, the usual people were there, Nancy Paterson, a number of investigators, and you were talking -- in fact, you were being questioned about a man who I'll come to later, but his name was Jozo Puskaric, Father Jozo Puskaric. And Nancy Paterson asked you this, and this was your reply, series of questions that I will put -- questions and answers that I will put to you. Sorry, Defence counsel should know it's page 1551 of that interview. Nancy Paterson: "So it sounds that he was being detained because he was valuable for exchange, not because he was found with weapons or was conspiring against the government or anything like that." And you answered, "To be honest, I don't know why he was arrested or who brought him in but I know, all I know, that he was at the police station, and that they told me at the Crisis Staff that we must not release him because, in exchange for him, we can get either a large number of Serbs or an officer from the Army of Republika Srpska, if any are captured in Croatia, because the whole time, there was this sword of Damocles hanging over us, the problem of about 3.000 Serbs captured in Odzak. That is the information I received from Zaric and others who maintained communication with that side, and that was a hard problem." Then Nancy Paterson asked you this question, and you gave this answer, and this is what I'm really interested in: "That raises the question: How much power and authority did you have as a police chief to release people who were being detained? Could you make that decision on your own or did you have to get permission from the Crisis Staff?" Answer: "I had to seek approval from the Crisis Staff." You maintain that position?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And when bigger groups were involved or more important people like this person Puskaric, I could not pass -- make the decision myself, but that doesn't mean that on a few occasions which involved less important persons, which I released and I later had problems with staff and the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. So in the case of the more important people, they would be involved in the decision making. In the case of less important personages, you would have the discretion to operate by yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On a few occasions, for these less important people, on my own initiative, I made such a gesture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you mentioned earlier, in an answer that you just gave, that you occasionally had problems with the Crisis Staff and with the army over releasing people. What sort of problems did you experience?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I had problems with members of the army, not the Crisis Staff, but on two or three occasions, with the army. And if need be, I can also explain these two or three cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that won't be necessary. That won't be necessary, Mr. Todorovic. I want to ask you some questions about Mr. Simo Zaric now, and perhaps before I do, I should produce this document to you. MR. DI FAZIO: For the benefit of Defence colleagues, they will know of this document as document C29.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just have a read of the document, please. All right. Have you acquainted yourself? First of all, signature, any idea whose signature it is?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it looks like the signature of Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the national security service that's referred to in the beginning of the document?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be in fact the secret police or the national security, national security [As interpreted]. These were the terms which were being used in the Republika Srpska and in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was envisaged as the role of chief of National Security Service by the Crisis Staff? What did they expect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just to intervene for the transcript, when mentioning what were the terms used for this body, he said "secret police," then he said "state security" and "national security." And it was here in the transcript, it's page 19, row 23, it says twice "national security, national security." Actually, he said "state security."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, you can clear that. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, just a minor problem with the transcript. When I asked you to describe national security service, you said, "It's the secret police, state security and national security." Is that the way you described it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said these were the three terms which were used, being used for the same service. Somebody called this the service of national security, of state security, or the secret police. However, that was one service, but these three terms were used in the public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Now, what did the Crisis Staff have in mind would be the areas to be covered, the zone of responsibility, for this position? What was his brief, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say I don't know what the Crisis Staff planned or what they were thinking about when they passed this decision. However, the issue of national security that are -- these are secret activities, and they are older than issues and activities of public security. At least that was -- that's the practice in Republika Srpska and in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I follow you. What do you mean that national security, secret activities, are older than issues of public security? I don't quite follow you. Do you mean they are more important or something like that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that -- I said that it had greater competences and that it is superior to the public security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. All right. The document describes in paragraph 1 Mr. Simo Zaric as being an economist. How does that description sit with you, as an economist? Did you ever know him to be an economist?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't work with him on economic matters and I didn't see his degree, but I did hear that in his mature age that he acquired a degree from the faculty in Brcko, and I also know that he also worked for quite some time in the state security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 2 says that his duties shall be carried out in accordance with the guidelines of the Crisis Staff. Did you ever see any such guidelines or are you aware of any such guidelines pertaining to the chief of national security?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I personally did not see his -- his reports, but -- and I wasn't personally there, whether he was giving them or not, whether he was receiving instructions in different meetings or submitting reports in these meetings, I don't know because I wasn't there. Because this was, after all, a secret police and I was a chief of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. Okay. You may not have been present. Did you ever hear that he provided reports or spoke to the Crisis Staff about his activities?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard that he had discussions and that he tried to organise this service of national security again, and this is what he was working on for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn of the -- his appointment?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about his appointment in my office when Mr. Zaric brought this decision and he said to me, "From today on, I am the chief for national security." And I asked him, "Who appointed you?" And he said, "I was appointed by the Crisis Staff," and then he showed me this document. And I asked him, "What do you mean, the Crisis Staff? I'm also a member of the Crisis Staff." And he said, "You have nothing to worry about. As you can see, there is a stamp and a signature of the president of the Crisis Staff here, and from now on, I am the national security chief."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you speak to anyone regarding that appointment, after he came and told you this?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think I talked to Mr. Blagoje Simic and he also said that this document was an original, and that he was indeed appointed to this position and that he would be doing the job that goes with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 3 says that, "The chief of national security shall be fully accountable to the Crisis Staff." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what that means? If you don't know, say so, but have you got any idea what that might mean?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I can say anything particular about this, but from this article, we can see that he is fully accountable to the Crisis Staff, to which he has to submit reports about his work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Before I move on to my next question, I'd like you to note that the date of the document is the 29th of April, 1992. I'm going to ask you some questions about the period of time preceding that. MR. DI FAZIO: And if Your Honours please, I'd like to now produce that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be P81 ter for the B/C/S and P81, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, could I ask a short question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have a short break? I would like to use the lavatories, just for a couple of minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We shall rise for ten minutes. --- Break taken at 10.06 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We continue with the Prosecution. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Todorovic, I want to ask you about the period of time preceding the appointment of Mr. Zaric as chief of national security. My first question is, did he participate in any way in the arrests? I don't necessarily mean going out and laying hands on people but in any way at all in the arrests that started after the 17th.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way did he participate?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, during the first days or even maybe the first two months, worked in my police station as a criminal investigator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's in the SUP building facing the TO building?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have an office there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he attend on a daily basis or on a more infrequent basis? Can you give us any idea?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came very often. He didn't spend the whole -- his whole day there in the station, but he would come very often and he was -- he would conduct his investigation, take statements, and based on his knowledge from before April 17th and also during the interrogation, he would give suggestions to the other criminal investigators and police officers that certain people be taken into custody and that investigations be conducted about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever participate in questioning suspects?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, can you give us an idea of the frequency of that? Was that an infrequent occurrence or was it a fairly regular thing?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first days, it happened quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His office, was it on the first or second floor? Perhaps I should clarify that. We have a slightly elevated floor, I believe, in the SUP. You go up some stairs and that's what I'll call the first floor. And then there is a second floor at least. Now which floor was his office on?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the second floor, there was more than one office that the criminal investigators used, and Mr. Zaric worked in one of these offices as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, before you proceed with your line of questioning, I would like you to re-examine your question on page 24, line 29, when you asked the witness: "Did he ever participate in questioning suspects?" And the witness answered: "Yes, yes, he did." What do you mean by "suspects"? MR. DI FAZIO: I see. I'll clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that Mr. Zaric did participate in questioning suspects. Were these people who had been arrested by your police or 4th Detachment members?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, he participated in questioning those that were taken into custody, those that were in the police station, and those people might have been taken to the police either by 4th Detachment members or by police members, police officers, but regardless of that, we are talking about the Muslims and Croats that were already located in the police station and he would question them and take their statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. While we are still on this topic, I think your evidence is that, quickly, this wasn't enough room in the SUP building for the prisoners and so a number were moved over to the TO building. Can you recall if he ever questioned any prisoners who were brought over from the TO for questioning? To put the matter at its simplest, did he ever question people who were taken out of custody from the TO building and/or the cells in the SUP building and question them?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any specific details at this moment, but all the men that were taken into custody and were kept, either in the SUP building or the TO building, or later in the primary school building. Then policemen would take them to the offices of the criminal investigation service, where the criminal investigators were, and this is where Mr. Zaric worked for a while, and then their statements would be taken. MR. DI FAZIO: Does that satisfy Your Honour's query?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I wanted to ask you about the positioning of Mr. Zaric's office. It was on the second floor, you say. Was it facing the TO building or facing the river, the Sava?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those three offices that were used by the criminal investigators and Mr. Zaric had windows facing the TO building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have a clear view of the TO building from his office?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be more specific, did he have a clear view of the yard of the TO building?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You had a clear view of the TO yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, I'm going to ask you in more detail about the issue of exchanges at a later point in time, but can you just briefly tell us, first of all, if exchange lists, lists of prisoners to be exchanged, were created? First of all, you can just tell us "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, lists were created, lists of prisoners who were going to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zaric, to your knowledge, ever participate in the creation of such lists?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he participated in creating the first two or three lists. That's what I saw. But it might be possible that he also participated in the creation of others. However, I did not see that, but I do know that he participated in the creation of the first two or three lists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got any idea if those lists in which you know he did participate in creating included any of the prisoners who were in the TO building and in the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the period of time leading up to his appointment as chief of national security, did he have a particular rank or -- yes, a particular rank, in the -- in his work?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean a rank in the police?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. When he was working in his office, leading up to the 29th of April, before the 29th of April, what was his position? What would you describe it, an investigator or chief of investigator? What precisely was his rank?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have ranks in the police at the time, only soldiers. The military had ranks. But he was an investigator, a criminal investigator. The first days, he wanted to become the chief of the criminal investigation service. That's how he behaved. But I told him orally, "You can work as an investigator in the criminal investigation service but the chief of the criminal investigation service is Milos Savic, attorney at law, who even before the war worked in this police station as a criminal investigator."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that he wanted in the first days to be chief of the criminal investigation services. I'd just like you to expand on that a bit. How do you know that he wanted to be that? Did you have any discussions with him? Was the issue raised between you both?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first few days, he behaved as if he was the chief of the criminal investigation service, but then I told him that Milos Savic was responsible for that service, that he was the chief of that service, and I told him, "You, however, can work as a criminal investigator within this criminal investigations service where -- whose chief is Milos Savic." And I told him this orally. There was no document written about it or anything, or there was no document about the organisation or reorganisation of this service. And then he just continued working there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this issue a source of friction between you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there might have been some friction. He had a very high opinion about himself and his police work, and that's how he behaved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move just briefly to more specific issues. Do you know a man named -- nicknamed "Coner"?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you here. When you asked about whether or not there might have been -- there was some friction between the witness and Mr. Accused Simo Zaric, his answer was, "Well, there might have been some friction." This is an important point, I think. I would like to have a specific answer from the witness whether there was friction between the two of them or there wasn't any friction. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll -- we'll clarify that and I also think that there might be evidence later in his testimony regarding this general issue. But I'll ask Mr. Todorovic again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Her Honour wants to know with some more -- some greater accuracy, did the issue of Mr. Zaric's appointment or lack of appointment as chief of the investigators actually lead to words between you, to coldness between you, lack of cooperation, or hostility between you? Can you try and be a bit more specific?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't notice any hostility. He was displeased but only a little, and he showed his displeasure but not much, and he just continued working as he pleased. He worked in the police station. He would also go to the brigade, and he also did a lot of things by himself. But then later he would inform me of some of his actions and of some of his actions he would not inform me, but I can't really say that there was any open hostility between us. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the man Coner, do you know his full name?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know his name and surname. I knew the person just as Coner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A man of Muslim ethnicity, I believe?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a Muslim, and on the basis of Zaric's information submitted to me, he was in the -- within the narrower group of the SDS [as interpreted] which was working on the procurement of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he ever arrested by the police?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you play a part in his arrest? By that I don't necessarily mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, just an intervention to the transcript. His answer was, in page 30, line -- between line 3 and 5 - it's probably error in typing - it's not "SDS." The witness said SDA party. And it was not a narrower group, it was the inner circle of the SDA party. That's what he said. But my friend can clarify that with the witness, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, before we break, Mr. Di Fazio, can you just clarify that so we have a correct record on the transcript. MR. DI FAZIO: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This man Coner, I don't think you meant to say that he was in the SDS. I think you meant SDA, did you not? And secondly, did you say that he was in the inner circle, the inner circle of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that he belonged to the SDA party and that he was in the -- in this inner circle of the leadership of the SDA, and that he participated in the arming of Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We shall take our break now and resume our proceedings at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution is continuing. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, just before the break, I was asking you about the man Coner, and I was about to ask you -- I wanted to ask you if you played a part in his arrest. I don't necessarily mean physically going out and getting him but instructing people to do so, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I received the information from Mr. Zaric that Mr. Coner had an important role in the arming, and on the basis of this information, and his insistence, the police then arrested, apprehended, Mr. Coner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Did he actually speak to you about picking up -- sorry, arresting Mr. Coner? Sorry, the man Coner?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And following that, were instructions given to police to go out and arrest him?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After that, the police arrested Coner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far you've described arrests being conducted by the 4th Detachment, your police officers, and also paramilitaries. Did Nikolic ever send any prisoners to you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It happened on a few occasions. I remember that on a bus, they brought in some 30, 40 people, and I was told that they were sent by Commander Nikolic and to place them and house them in the TO building, which also then happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these 30 or 40 people Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Do you know what area they were from? Were they from the town of Bosanski Samac or were they people who had been picked up in the outlying areas of the municipality or, indeed, anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of my information, they were from the areas of -- arrested in the area of Orasje, and some of them were born and lived in the municipality of Teslic, but at the time, they were in this first area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Nikolic supply you or did anyone else supply you with any information, specifics, specific details, regarding what these people had done, why they'd been arrested?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, I didn't -- I did not receive any detailed information about their criminal activity, just I was told that Commander Nikolic called -- arrested them and that I should hold them in detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And presumably, they were duly held in detention. Do you know where? Was it the TO, the SUP, or high school gym, primary school gym? Where? Where did you put them?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I remember, one part of them were put in the building of TO, and others in the elementary school, and as far as I remember, this was carried out by the commander of the police station and his assistants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I wonder whether Mr. Todorovic could clarify -- sorry, okay. It's line 8, page 32. The end of his answer, Mr. Todorovic says, "They were in this first area." I'd like to know exactly what is meant by that, because in your question, you had mentioned the town, were they picked up in the town of Bosanski Samac or were they picked up in outlying areas of municipality. So this first area, is it the town? So if you could clarify, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, one of my earlier questions was about the bus load of people, and I asked you if they were picked up in Bosanski Samac or in the outlying areas of the municipality. You went on to explain that they came from the municipality of Teslic and some from Orasje, and you then said something that's not very clear. You said, "But at the time they were in this first area." I don't quite follow that. Is the first area something different from Orasje or Teslic, or were you just talking about Orasje?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it a matter of translation or I didn't express myself properly. As far as I know, they were arrested on the Serbian -- Serb territory, the outlying areas of Samac. The village where they were arrested belonged to the Serb Municipality of Orasje, which is a part of the territory of Samac, and I heard that some were born and earlier lived in Teslic, but at that moment in time, they happened to be there where they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff must have had a headquarters somewhere. Where did it set up its headquarters, initially?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, the Crisis Staff moved from two or three locations. First, it had its headquarters in the agricultural industry, then in the offices of the district heating plant, and then in the municipality building, which is in the centre of the town. MR. DI FAZIO: Can Your Honours just bear with me for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Can the witness be shown the photographs, please? 14A, I think is the unmarked bundle.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm awfully sorry, Mr. Di Fazio, which exactly, the number of the photograph or all of them? MR. DI FAZIO: No, no. Just one particular photograph, number 20.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the Crisis Staff had its headquarters in the agricultural industry. Is that the building you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, this is not the building. It's the building in the same yard, and that that building is some ten metres further south, but in this same yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Okay. All right. Do you know what was in this building at the time that's depicted?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this building on the photo?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the green one with the pigeons on top.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, in the first few days, the commander of the tank battalion, or whatever it was called, that formation, they stayed -- they were quartered here with the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I've finished, Mr. Usher. In any event, Mr. Todorovic, the Crisis Staff headquarters was somewhere near that building, not -- very close by?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same courtyard, but only ten metres to the left of the gate entrance of this agri-business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did it shift after that, the headquarters of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, it moved to the business premises of the Uniglas factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's not an objection, it's just a suggestion to my learned friend. Maybe we could have a time frame, a period, so that we could follow these details. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm grateful to Mr. Pantelic, and I intend to establish that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you in the first -- sorry, how long was the Crisis Staff in the first location, the one near the agricultural industry plant?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, maybe the first five to seven days. I don't believe it was more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you -- the Crisis Staff moved to Uniglas?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, how long was the Crisis Staff housed at the Uniglas factory?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe 20 days or a month, but I'm not a hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where precisely in the Uniglas factory did it have its offices?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the office administration premises, where the director, the administration and the clerks had their offices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a canteen in that building?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that building, but in the yard of that factory, there was a canteen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For a period of time that the Crisis Staff was located in this building, were prisoners who were housed in the TO and the SUP and so on taken there for meals?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first few days, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I think maybe we should clarify Mr. Todorovic's answer on line 14: "On the first few days, yes." Does it mean on the first few days, let's say the 17th to the 19th of April, when the Crisis Staff was located in the -- near the agricultural building, or does the answer mean on the first few days when the Crisis Staff had moved into their second location, this factory with the canteen in the yard? MR. DI FAZIO: I understood him to be saying the latter but I'll clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If you could. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to we are absolutely certain, when you say the prisoners were taken for meals, are you referring to the period of time that the Crisis Staff was located in the Uniglas factory?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe for a few days, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking for the period of time. All I want to know is this: The canteen that you've mentioned, was that at the Uniglas factory?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's where the prisoners were taken for a short period of time to get their meals?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, it's not in dispute in this case that a number of locations sprang up around Bosanski Samac where prisoners were kept: The SUP, then the TO, and later the high school gym, and I believe the primary school gym for a period of time. Who was responsible for finding these locations to house these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for determining the locations, this was entrusted to me, the commander, the deputy commander of the police, and also our other aides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you keep other Crisis Staff members acquainted -- up to date, I should say, with the fact that more locations were needed and created for keeping the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were informed, the members of the Crisis Staff were informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution, Mr. Di Fazio. The answer has been given. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry, I should have told the Chamber I was just looking at a matter. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Todorovic, it's just a -- another portion of your interview that you gave on the 18th of January. I'll quickly go -- put something to you. Again, Nancy Paterson was asking you questions. MR. DI FAZIO: For the benefit of my learned friends, it's at the top of page 34 of the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Question by Nancy Paterson: "Again, you haven't really answered my question about the establishment of the camps. Who made these decisions to detain the men and put them in these particular locations?" Answer: "On the first nights, the first days, it was Nikolic who decided that. As the number of detainees rose, their number became too great to be accommodated in the existing premises and the Crisis Staff simply approved the process which was going on already." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I take it from that answer that the Crisis Staff was kept abreast of developments regarding the creation of new prison establishments?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they approved the continued process of creating new prisons as their swelling numbers increased?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. One of the prisoners was a man named Dikan, who was killed by Lugar. That's not in dispute. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was, I think, in the TO building when he was killed, was he not?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was his death made known to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there -- was his death discussed, the consequences and so on, was it discussed by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lugar was a paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I assume --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paramilitary, but at the time, he was within the framework of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. He was part of that initial group of 50 men which later became larger and was called the Special Battalion, I think; is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. The paramilitaries had access to the men in the TO building and the SUP -- or the TO building in particular?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff know that the paramilitaries had access to the prisoners from time to time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They knew that the paramilitaries would come in occasionally, although I issued an order for the police to prevent their entering the building, but this -- it was difficult to prevent it particularly if they had -- if they drank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All I want to know, though, is the Crisis Staff knew the paramilitaries were gaining access to the prisoners. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, the translation is somewhat different. The Crisis Staff knew that occasionally, without any permission and irrespective of my ban, that they entered these premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As part of your plea of guilty, you admitted causing -- killing a man called Antesa. I'm not interested in the details of that, how that came about. I'm, in fact, interested in the aftermath of that. Was the fact of the killing made known to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it discussed amongst members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, amongst some members of the Crisis Staff members, it was discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that include Dr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another event that concerned prisoners was the murder of a large number of people in Crkvina by Lugar.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that that occurred in early May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I suggested to you the 6th and 7th of May, does that sound right to you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know precisely, but it must -- it was somewhere around the 5th, 6th or 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These three episodes I've just asked you about, can you remember the sequence, Dikan, Antesa, and Crkvina? Can you remember in what sequence they occurred?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, the first unfortunate event concerned Dikan, then the most serious one in Crkvina, and somewhere in June or July, this tragic event concerning Antesa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I believe you omitted to ask the witness concerning the Crkvina killing, whether the Crisis Staff was informed. You did that for the first two events. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm going to get into that in full detail, Your Honour. I'm not leaving that for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact of the killings at Crkvina, was it a matter of common knowledge in the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first hear that it had occurred, and who informed you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened during the night, and the next day, I heard it for the first time from the commander of the police station, Savo Cancarevic. He informed me about this unfortunate event and he told me that they removed all the evidence, and they've taken care of it. He told -- I told him, "Why did they do that, as we were supposed to carry on an on-site inspection?" He said that Lugar was involved, who is the army and of the 17th Tactical Group, and that it was Lugar himself who insisted and ordered that the traces of this event be removed during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. And was -- were the bodies buried, concealed, somewhere?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cancarevic informed me that, on Lugar's orders, he found some villagers and that they took the bodies away, that they washed off the blood, but he did not take me -- tell me where these bodies were buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Was -- were you informed about a tractor being used from the Usce, I think it's Usce Bosne company, to dig a grave and place the bodies in there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, after a considerable amount of time, I found out in informal conversations that this piece of equipment was used from this company for digging out the hole where these unfortunate men were buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just answer my next question with a "yes" or a "no." Have you recently provided and assisted officers of the OTP in attempting to locate the bodies?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, you're asking me a difficult question. This is an open session, and these things are very serious. There have already been some threats against me, but I will -- but I will answer nevertheless. If there is a possibility to have a closed session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is it relevant? MR. DI FAZIO: It's not particularly relevant. I'd hoped to deal with it very briefly, if Your Honours please. I think it's a matter of some importance to the witness, but from the Prosecution's point of view, it's not particularly relevant to the matters in the indictment. May I leave the decision on this with the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, following the report to you by Savo Cancarevic, did you inform the Crisis Staff of what had happened in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they knew that Lugar was the man responsible?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was an investigation ever conducted?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and the members of my police station did not conduct an investigation, and I don't know about others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now, I want to leave this topic and move on to another topic, and that is the issue of the exchanges. Perhaps we will go from the specific to the general. First of all, may I ask you about Mr. Izet Izetbegovic? You've already said that you know him, and there is no dispute that he was amongst one of the first people to be arrested, nor is there any dispute that he was exchanged, but it's the circumstances that I want to ask you about. First of all, can you recall how it came about that the process of his exchange started?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, first interview was conducted in my office with a close relative of Izet Izetbegovic, Alija Izetbegovic, who at that time was the President of that part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who suggested that Mr. Izetbegovic be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, Mr. Zaric suggested that Izet Izetbegovic invite to call Alija Izetbegovic on the phone from my office, and to ask from Mr. Alija Izetbegovic to release three and-a-half or 4.000 Serbs who had already been arrested in the municipality of Odzak. This municipality was controlled by Croatian and Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone else speak to you about using him in an exchange? Was it just Mr. Zaric or did someone else speak to you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric talked not about the exchange but that Izet intervene or talk to his relative, Alija, so the Serbs that were detained be released. After some time, I was called from Belgrade and they said that they saw on their TV that Izet Izetbegovic was in the police station and that they -- and they were asking whether we wanted to give him to them, to send them to Belgrade, so that they could exchange him from Belgrade for 200 or 300 cadets, that is to say students, that were in the military academy in Rajlovac. This was an air force academy, and the Muslims kept these cadets detained in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
