utterances.text: Right. Do you know a man named Colonel Jeremic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jeremic called me on the phone and he said that -- what they had seen on the television, and he said that his superiors were asking to give them Izetbegovic so that he could be exchanged for the aforementioned young cadets who had been detained in Rajlovac, and that's what happened in the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this Jeremic a Belgrade personality? Did he work in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He worked in the air force in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did he speak to you personally?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He spoke to me personally on the phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did -- do you know if he spoke to Mr. Zaric about the matter or did he just deal with you on this issue?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he only talked to me. I don't think he talked to Zaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Mr. Izetbegovic taken out of custody during the course of negotiations?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm not quite sure what your question means, was he taken out of custody?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not very clear. I apologise. Was he brought over from the TO building into the offices of the SUP during the course of telephone calls and negotiations regarding his exchange, just transferred across the road to the SUP?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On -- in two or three occasions, he was transferred from the TO building to the SUP building, the police building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that for the purpose of these negotiations on his particular exchange?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I can remember, he was transferred so that he could give a statement, and once he was brought in because he had given an interview to a TV crew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But I'm not talking about those two occasions. I'm now just confining my questions to the exchange. Was he brought over specifically for negotiations with the exchange -- relating to the exchange?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, he was brought over to the police building so that he could give a statement and because of this -- the fact that he gave the interview to the TV crew, and while he was there, Zaric suggested that he should call Alija on the phone. As far as his exchange to Sarajevo was concerned, there were no discussions with him on that topic, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "Alija," you mean Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean his cousin Alija, who was the president at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was Alija Izetbegovic contacted by phone regarding the exchange?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was contacted, but I would like to add the following. Alija Izetbegovic was told that he should try to influence and work out the release of the Serbs from Odzak. As far as I can recall, there was no discussion with Alija regarding the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just not very clear in this. What was the role of Mr. Izet Izetbegovic in these negotiations? What did you want from him? What did Mr. Zaric want from him? What was his significance?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Izet and Alija are close relatives, and we thought that if Izet called Alija on the phone, he should ask him that Alija influence the Muslim-Croat formations in Odzak to release several thousand Serbs that had been detained there, and then we would release the rest of the Muslims and Croats, although at that time there weren't so many of them there, maybe about 100, but not more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the cadets in Serbia? Was that raised at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a suggestion to my learned friend. We are going into a little bit confused situation. Were the cadets in Serbia? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, sorry, perhaps that was a wrong assumption on my part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in the role --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just before you ask that question, just in case we move on to other things, could you not ask the witness directly, did Izet speak to Alija on the telephone, yes or no? Because we know everyone seemed to be talking about it but we don't know yes or no, did they actually connect. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is clear: Did he speak to -- did Izet Izetbegovic speak to Alija Izetbegovic on the phone?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Simo Zaric present when that occurred and were you present when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I was present, and a minute or two into the conversation, after the introduction -- introductory conversation of Izet and Alija, I took the receiver and then I talked to Alija Izetbegovic. Whether Zaric was there at that moment or not, I don't know, because he was -- he kept coming and going, so I don't know whether he was in this office at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say to Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told Alija Izetbegovic that the Croatian and Muslim units in the area of the municipality of Odzak arrested around 3500 Serbs and that I was asking him to release these Serbs from the camps because I wasn't sure that I, as a police chief, would be able to stop, to prevent the Serbs in the municipality of Samac from doing the same, from arresting Muslims and Croats. So in other words, I wanted to prevent a revenge. And at that moment, he said, "Well, you know, I have no control over this territory of Bosnia. They are listening to what Zagreb says, not to me." And then he said that, "I would tell my Minister of Interior Affairs, Alija Delimustafic, and he will get in touch with you." And after half an hour, his minister, Alija Delimustafic, did indeed call.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout the series of phone calls, or at least this first and second phone call, was the question of the exchange of Mr. Izet Izetbegovic ever raised, ever discussed?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, specific issues of the exchange of Izet Izetbegovic was not mentioned, I think, but when Izet phoned him, he said, "Hello, Alija. I have been arrested. I'm here in the police station in Samac. I have been arrested along with the larger number belonging to the leadership of the Party of Democratic Action. Please, could you influence these men in Odzak to release the Serbs so that we could prevent and stop this evil?" As far as I can recall, there was no concrete talks about us releasing Izet and them releasing the others. That's all I can remember at this moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm going to leave this topic, Mr. Todorovic. I want to continue on asking you about exchanges. And I want to ask you now about Father Puskaric. I just want to put to you some passages from the interview that was conducted with you on the 8th of January, 2001. MR. DI FAZIO: For the benefit of Defence counsel, the passages I'm interested in are at pages 50 and 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Again, I do apologise, is it 8 or 18 of January? MR. DI FAZIO: Eight. Eighteen, my mistake, one-eight, 18th of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nancy Paterson was again asking you questions and you were answering, and she put to you this passage, and I want to ask you about it. "I'd like to talk to you now about Simo Zaric some more and this incident that happened with Catholic priest, Father Puskaric. First, can you explain why Father Puskaric, who was a Roman Catholic priest, got arrested and detained at the police station and later at the Territorial Defence building? And you answered, "Well, believe me, I'm not clear on that point either. I know that he was arrested and I know that he was at the police station, but who brought him there and under whose orders, I don't know." Nancy Paterson then asked you: "What's the reason why you, as the police chief," then something that wasn't picked up by the recording machine was said. She continued: "... or didn't look into this matter to find out what the circumstances were?" And you answered, "Well, it was much easier to find yourself in the police station than to get out of it. I know that somebody brought him there and I was told that he was very valuable and that I should not release him for that reason because, in exchange for him, we could get 100 or 200 from Odzak." Now, it's that last answer of yours that I'm interested in. Can you recall who told you he was valuable?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People in the Crisis Staff told me about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they explain that his value lay in being able to exchange him for a lot more people, 100 or 200 people from Odzak? That's where his value lay?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 100 or 200 people or for a Republika Srpska army officer who might have fallen into their hands. When I say "their hands," I mean Muslims or Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Subsequently, were negotiations in fact conducted regarding the exchange of Puskaric?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who conducted those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The negotiations were, generally speaking, conducted by Mr. Tadic and two other members of this commission. And when you're talking about Puskaric, I know that Mr. Zaric, on two or three occasions, took Mr. Puskaric to the building where the radio station is and that he talked to people from Odzak, and that he tried to get Puskaric to influence these people with his authority that they released the Serbs that they held in camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at this document that I produce to you, please. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, Defence counsel will know of it as C75.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Todorovic, just acquaint yourself with the general nature of the document and then I'll take you to specific portions to see who signed it, who it's addressed to. Cast your eye over the content. And perhaps my first question should be is this -- the author is apparently Mitar Mitrovic. I think you've mentioned him before.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The letter is dated the 17th of June, 1992. Was he on the Crisis Staff at that time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, the stamp, it appears to be the usual Crisis Staff stamp. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a clear copy but it looks like the stamp used by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get to the content of the letter, can I ask you this? Do you know a man named Petar Andjelovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know him personally but I heard about this priest, but personally, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was a priest. Did he have any connection with Father Puskaric?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in his position, he was superior to Puskaric in the church hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's exactly what I wanted to know, thank you. Following Puskaric's arrest, did anyone try to gain his release?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This friar, Petar Andjelovic, probably wrote a letter to the Patriarch Pavle and that he asked and requested that Puskaric be released

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Patriarch Pavle. I'm sorry, Mr. Todorovic, I don't know much about the hierarchy of the Orthodox Church. Is he based in Belgrade and does he hold a very high position in the Orthodox Church?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is in Belgrade, and he is the head of the Orthodox Church of the entire former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, obviously, a man of -- who had considerable rank in the Orthodox Church?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the highest possible position in the Orthodox Church of Serbia and of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did he communicate with the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he personally, but from what I've heard, a letter had been sent from the Holy Synod in Belgrade. And in fact, this is either a response to that letter or some telephone call.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you had received information that the Orthodox Patriarch had somehow contacted the Crisis Staff, either by letter or by phone? Is that your position? And that this letter that you have before you is the response to that inquiry?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this matter, the inquiry by the Patriarch in Belgrade and the release of Father Jozo Puskaric, a matter treated as a matter of some importance by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Importance was attributed to this appeal made by Patriarch Pavle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In particular, did the Crisis Staff, Crisis Staff members, regard it as a matter of some importance?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the majority of the members considered that this appeal by the patriarch is of importance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And thus, this letter was created that you have before you, by Mitar Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The letter says, in the third paragraph, that Jozo Puskaric was in temporary isolation. Can you comment on that? Do you know if that's true or not?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was detained on a -- temporarily in the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would be fair if my learned friend would not take the words out of context because he has certain objections prior to that. Because of the proceedings, maybe he could just make the mention of the word prior to that word that he mentioned so that we have a much clearer picture of the parts of this particular document. Otherwise, it's the endless story, taking the words out of context and then, in our cross, we shall do the same. And it's for the benefit of this time in these proceedings. MR. DI FAZIO: I certainly want to avoid taking words out of context if I can, but I'm not sure what Mr. Pantelic is driving at. The line there, at least in the English, says, "Puskaric is being remanded in custody and in temporary isolation." I don't know if that means he was separated from other prisoners or not, and that's what I'm really interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think, Mr. Pantelic, you can deal with the matter in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, but let me just make a short -- Mr. Di Fazio said it was temporary isolation. Now he's introducing another word, which changes completely the sense. That was the basis for my suggestion. Line 10, that was his word, "temporary isolation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can you leave it with the Prosecution to deal with their case as they see fit? You will have the opportunity in cross-examination to deal with your case as you will see fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Di Fazio, please continue. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, all I really want to know about that line is this. It says: "The former has been remanded in custody, namely, is in temporary isolation." All I want to know is -- we all agree he was in custody but all I want to know is, was he separated from the other prisoners and kept in some sort of isolation? Because that's how I read it, and if I'm not correct, then I want to know. Was he isolated from the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was not isolated, nor was he given some special treatment. He was in custody but he wasn't particularly isolated with more severe measures applied to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, there seems to be, in the first two paragraphs, some contradiction to me, and I just want to be absolutely clear. The second paragraph says, he's "not imprisoned because imprisonment implies subjecting a person to slavery without any hope of survival in this world." Yet, in the next paragraph, it says he's been remanded in custody. Now, I don't want to quibble about the words. All I want to know is this: Was Father Jozo Puskaric arrested and kept in prison? Was that the plain situation?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Friar Jozo Puskaric was detained and he was in the police station and in the TO building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness said that Friar Jozo Puskaric was detained on remand, which is a great difference in terms of legal category than "was detained." He was detained on remand. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. We must be precise, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And I will endeavour to be as precise as I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say that Father Jozo Puskaric was detained on remand?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, during this period of remand, did he have many court appearances, private consultations with his lawyer, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he didn't -- had no court appearances, and as far as I know, he did not have a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, are we going to find out what he was accused of? MR. DI FAZIO: Good question, if Your Honour pleases. I hadn't asked that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what he was picked up for, what he was accused of?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the question of Mrs. Paterson, I said I didn't know who brought him in and what he was accused of. But later, I believe he was accused of participating in the organisation of an armed rebellion. It was assumed that, in the warehouses of the church, there would be weapons and ammunition. We didn't find any ammunition. We found, however, a lot of food and medical materials. And he was -- the accusation was that he was participating in the preparation of an armed insurgence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, you commented upon this very issue in your interview of the 3rd of April, 2001. Again, on this occasion, you were being asked a question by an investigator, Mr. Tore Soldal, questions about this very letter, this very document. And he asked you, "What kind of offence are we talking about here?" And you said this: "The fact is that Jozo Puskaric was detained. At the time army and police operated jointly, and there was information that in this storage of the church in which Jozo Puskaric worked, there was a warehouse. There was large amounts of food, oil and ammunition. It later turned out that there were no large amounts of ammunition. There were just large amounts of food." Would you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, that is what I said previously in my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And I do apologise, for the purposes of Defence counsel, this is page 38 and 39 of the -- of that interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And still when he was dealing with this issue, the investigator asked you: "How long time did you actually need to find out this?" He's Norwegian; that might explain the sentence. You replied, "In normal circumstances, this would have been discovered very quickly. In conditions of war, I don't know how long it took. Certainly not so much time, time he spent in custody." Then the investigator asked you, "For me, it looks like the Patriarch wanted you to release this man. Then it would be quite easy to do a search on his premises to see whether he had ammunition or not." You said, "Yes, not much time were needed but unfortunately he spent a lot of time there." Did you say that in the course of the interview?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the case, then, that early on in the period of Puskaric's detention, it became clear that he hadn't had -- he hadn't got ammunition stored in his house or his -- in his house?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I didn't understand the question. Or did you pose a question to me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry if I didn't make it clear. What I mean is, Puskaric spent some time in custody. Is it the case that early on in the period of his custody, it became clear that he didn't have ammunition kept at his house?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning, it was very quickly determined that there was no ammunition there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's move back to the original topic, which is the question of his exchange. Were negotiations conducted with people in Odzak regarding his exchange?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, and I mentioned that Mr. Zaric, two or three times, took Mr. Puskaric from the TO building to the other building with the radio transmitter, and they established communication with the responsible people in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on how many occasions -- I'm sorry, you said this took place two or three times. Was Mr. Zaric always the one conducting the negotiations or did Mr. Tadic involve himself as well?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told on -- that on those -- or two or three occasions, the commander or the deputy commander, that it was Zaric who took Puskaric for these talks. But I wasn't in the building and I wasn't involved. Now, who was present, who were all the people present, I don't know, but I know that Zaric and Puskaric were involved in these concrete cases, two or three cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you were responsible for the prisoners and so on, jointly with the Crisis Staff. Did Mr. Simo Zaric clear with you, in other words get your permission, to take Jozo Puskaric out of custody, over to the radio transmitters, to start these negotiations or did he take him out of custody himself, without consulting you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he didn't ask me about that. And I was only informed by the commander or the deputy commander that Zaric took this person there, and he didn't have to ask my permission for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zaric command sufficient authority such that he could take out prisoners if he wished, for whatever purposes, for example, the exchange purposes?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he did have this possibility to go in to talk, to take somebody out and to take him for the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours please, I seek to produce --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even -- even he took a group of 30, 40 people to the barracks in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, would Your Honours just give me a moment to consult with my colleague?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, thank you. I seek to produce into evidence the letter of Mitar Mitrovic. Perhaps it could be referred to as the letter to the Belgrade Patriarch dated the 17th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be P82 ter for the B/C/S and P82 for the English version, Your Honours. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, still on the issue of exchanges. I've been asking you about Mr. Zaric thus far. What about Mr. Miroslav Tadic, did he involve himself in exchanges?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic was the person who mainly led these exchanges, with another two or three people who were also in the commission -- exchange commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long was he engaged in this process of the exchange commission and the exchanges itself -- themselves?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly up to autumn, 1992, and later, I heard that the main person involved in exchanges was Captain Grujicic from the 1st Krajina Corps and who had the competence over this entire northern part of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Very soon after the takeover of -- or the commencement of hostilities around the 16th and 17th, were a small number of Croat and Muslim soldiers killed and their bodies left on a bridge?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It happened on the 1st or the 2nd day. It was either the 17th, 18th or 19th of April when the attempt was made, they made the attempt to enter Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened to the bodies of those particular -- of those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bodies -- at the insistence of the representatives of the Muslim and Croat forces in -- from Odzak, on their insistence to stop the fighting and to have an exchange of these bodies for two or three Serb soldiers which were there on that territory. So this was the first exchange which took place, and that is how the exchanges began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who participated in that particular exchange?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, Miroslav Tadic and I believe another person with him, but I do not -- maybe Ljubomir Cordasevic or Sveto Vasovic, somebody from the Red Cross of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were prisoners who were kept in the TO, the SUP, high school gyms, from time to time taken to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Tadic involved in those exchanges?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to organise, carry out those exchanges, did he need access to the prisons, TO, the SUP, the high school gym and so on?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First he had talks via that radio transmitter with the Muslims and Croats from Odzak, and he coordinated with them the list of people who they would be releasing from Odzak and whom they were requesting from Samac. And so Tadic coordinated with that other commission from Odzak. And he contacted with the -- these people that the Muslims and Croats were asking for and who were being detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the Croats and Muslims asked for a particular person, how would Mr. Tadic know if they were in custody or not?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he would ask, inquire, who of these people were -- where are these people that are being requested by Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ask who? Ask you or your officers?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the commander, deputy commanders, would submit to him the lists of people, of detainees, and then -- so that he knew that the people were either detained or they are not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these were the lists that, I suppose, the -- your department kept and he was provided with those lists? Is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was a book in which the names of all the detainees were registered, and the commander and deputy commanders would show this list of detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Chamber that Mr. Zaric had sufficient authority to gain access from time to time to the prisons. Did Mr. Tadic enjoy the same degree of authority?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tadic would contact the commander, deputy commander, and he could enter these premises to talk to the people who the Croats and Muslims asked to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I think now is the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will take our break now and resume our proceedings at 12.50 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Examination-in-chief continuing. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, you were talking about Miroslav Tadic and his role in the exchanges. Did he from time to time report, either formally or informally, to the Crisis Staff about how that was going?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to put to you a passage that occurred in your interview of the 4th of April, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe it's a little bit two-barrelled question, "formally or informally," and he said "Yes." What is formally or informally? Maybe we could clarify that. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, certainly. I think Mr. Pantelic has a point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I failed to clarify that with you, Mr. Todorovic. Did Miroslav Tadic provide formal reports or informal reports, or both?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a lawyer so I don't quite understand the terminology used, but as far as I can remember, Mr. Tadic occasionally gave oral reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that at meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were present?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he would inform the Crisis Staff -- my question is this: Would he inform the Crisis Staff of what was going -- what was happening, how it was -- the whole process was proceeding?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't give any details but I remember that he would usually give a report when an exchange finished. Afterwards, he would give his impressions. He would do this orally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And while we are still on this topic, I want to put to you this passage, as I said, from the 4th of April, 2001. MR. DI FAZIO: For the purposes of Defence counsel, they will find the passage at pages 33 -- at the bottom of page 33, top of page 34 of that interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Nancy Paterson asked you this and you gave this answer. Question by Nancy Paterson: "You said that Blagoje had some say in who got put on the list and who wasn't put on the list. Now, I know that exchanges were going on for a period of time, were going on fairly regularly. Once a week, once every two weeks, there was an exchange happening. Now let's talk through how this would work. Would Miroslav Tadic draw up, say, the first list of people that were being -- who he felt should be released in the next exchange and then would Blagoje have an opportunity to review that list and say, "This person can go, that person needs to stay?" And you answered, "He looked at some lists and I know that they consulted, that he consulted with Tadic. I don't know if he looked at every single list every time." Is that a fair representation of the role of Mr. Blagoje Simic in this exchange process?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that exchanges started in the first few months after -- after April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Di Fazio, before the witness answers, I think you need to be more specific. Because we've had evidence of what was alleged to be exchanges prior to April 1992, somewhere within the Prosecution case, and I think it's better if you are speaking about the Muslims and Croats who were arrested at the beginning of the conflict and thereafter, are you referring to them, their exchanges, or are you referring to the exchanges of other people or just generally? If you could be more specific. MR. DI FAZIO: The only reason I'm not being specific, if Your Honour pleases, is because I don't want to dwell on the topic. I don't want to have to put documentation relating to a particular exchange to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, that may not be necessary, but at least if we are sure of which people we are talking about, which exchanges, exchanges concerning which people. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, I see. I understand. I do apologise. I'm now with Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that was perhaps inaccurate of me, Mr. Todorovic. As far as the exchanges involving detained prisoners in Bosanski Samac, the Croats and Muslims who were detained in Bosanski Samac are concerned, their exchanges commenced in the first few months, first few weeks indeed, after the events of the 16th and 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, months later, was there an exchange commission formed?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please look at this document that I produce to you? MR. DI FAZIO: Before it's shown to the witness, can I just -- when it's been dealt with, can I just have a look at the B/C/S original, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Prosecutor tell us what number this document is so that we could find it as well? Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I apologise. C81.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, I won't be long on this document as all. Just quickly look at the signature. Again, can you comment?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it resembles the signature of the President, Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. And the document speaks for itself. It says that the War Presidency decided to appoint a committee for the exchange of prisoners, and you can see that the members of this committee include a number of people, including Mr. Tadic. You see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the other two men mentioned, Velimir Maslic and Simo Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Velimir Maslic worked for the municipality, in the Department for Social Activities. I think that's what it was called. Simo Nikolic was in the security part of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, and he was a member of this committee on behalf of that brigade, and throughout all the exchanges, there was always one member from this security section of the 2nd Posavina Brigade present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And Article 3 says that this committee had to provide monthly reports on exchanges of prisoners to the War Presidency. Do you say that, in fact, Mr. Tadic was providing reports even before he was required to do so, pursuant to this decision? And they are the oral reports you mentioned just earlier.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that, from time to time, he submitted oral reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Following the creation of this exchange commission, do you know if he continued to provide oral reports or did he provide -- start to provide written reports, or both, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he submitted oral -- he continued to submit oral reports from time to time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I produce the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be P83 and P83 ter, Your Honours. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any fee involved -- I'll withdraw that. Did people who were exchanged ever pay money to get exchanged?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since at that time there were a lot of misinformation floating around, I heard that there were some people who offered money to Mr. Tadic. I tried to figure out what was going on, and I asked this one man that was talking about it, "Do you want to be a witness so that I can start an investigation?" And he said, "No." Then I said, "Well, then, don't spread rumours if you're not ready to testify on them." This is with regard to Mr. Tadic. But I knew of another event that has to do with another man, but I don't know whether you would be interested in that. If you ask me, I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll just put a passage to you from your interview of the 6th of November, 2000. MR. DI FAZIO: For the purposes of Defence counsel, they will find the passage at page 54.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were being asked questions by an investigator. The investigator asked you: "As you most probably know, several witnesses claim that Tadic asked for money to put people on the exchange list. Do you know anything about that?" And you answered, "Well, I heard that being said but when I tried to get those people to give a statement to testify, they wouldn't do it. So I heard it as a story but I have no proof of it. I also heard that Fadil Topcagic was forging IDs for Croats and Muslims, to take them across the Drina and help them get away to Western Europe, and I tried it put a stop to that operation but again I wasn't able to prove it." The first part of your answer is what interests me. You said that you heard of Mr. Tadic taking money. From whom did you receive that information? What was your source of information?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this -- right at this moment, I cannot remember my source of information but as I've already said, there were a lot of rumours and lies floating around. And as I said in my previous answer, I wanted to start an investigation so I asked this man to help me, and he refused. So then I told him, "Well, don't assign blame to somebody if you don't know that what you're saying is true and you refuse to participate in an investigation that would prove whether these rumours and allegations were true or not."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I want to produce another document to the witness. The document will be known to Defence counsel as C89. If Your Honours please, I think the usher may be missing part of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Todorovic, I'll be very brief with this document. I don't want to dwell on it for long. You can immediately have a look at it and you can see that it's a decision appointing someone else to the exchange commission. That person is Simeun Simeunovic. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This copy is quite bad. I don't know who Simeun Simeunovic is. I know that there is a man called Simeon Simic but I don't know who Simeun Simeunovic is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the signature quite bad on your copy?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's quite bad. You can't even see the stamp very well. MR. DI FAZIO: Given those circumstances, if Your Honours please, I don't propose to produce that into evidence. If you wish, the matter can be marked -- the document can be marked for identification so we keep custody of it and we know what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the numbers for identification only?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be P84 ID and P84 ter ID, Your Honours. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another document that I want to produce to you on the issue of exchanges, Mr. Todorovic. MR. DI FAZIO: And for the benefit of Defence counsel, they will know of it as C70.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, can you just quickly look at the signature and tell us if it appears to be that of Dr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also a bad copy but the signature does resemble the signature of Mr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The order refers to the temporary accommodation of people who came in from Odzak, who were exchanged from Odzak, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As a matter of qualification, it's not order, it's conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, that's the title on the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And I beg your pardon, now it's confused me totally. C70 is conclusion of War Presidency dated, I suppose, 23rd November of 1992. Maybe it's some kind of misunderstanding. MR. DI FAZIO: No, I hope we have all got the same document. We need to clarify that straight away. First of all, Mr. Usher, may I see a copy of the document that's being presented to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because in that case, it might be order but it's not C70 document. It's conclusion. MR. DI FAZIO: I think what's happened here is the case manager gave me the wrong document, but let's start again. For the purpose of Defence counsel, C70 is the document that I'm interested in. It's entitled "Order on the Implementation of the Decision of the Crisis Staff on Temporary Housing of Exchanged Persons." That's the document that I have as C70. It's on the 65 ter list. Is that the document that Your Honours have or do you have some other document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, this is a different document. MR. DI FAZIO: There has been a mistake. I just ask the Chamber to be patient while we get it. It won't take a moment. If Your Honours please, I regret to say we don't have copies of this at the moment. I can give you my case manager's copy. Might I just show it to you briefly now and then produce --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we can look at it. MR. DI FAZIO: I apologise for the hiccup in the provision of these documents. Mr. Usher? May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can proceed. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Could you just have a look at that document?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise any signature?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's a poor copy but it resembles the signature of Mr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have just a few very brief questions about this document. First of all, Article 3 refers to a First Lieutenant Ljubomir M. Tadic. That is not, I believe, the defendant in this case, Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It does not refer to Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Article 1 says that the individuals who came from Odzak will be given temporary accommodation in Hasici, MZ. Before April 16 and 17, was that a Croat village?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I tender the document, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, am I to keep counsel's copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Copies for the registry are available, aren't they? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes. Those copies can be tendered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They will be P85 and P85 ter, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, I want to now move away from the question of exchange to another topic now, and that is, the question of people working in the Bosanski Samac municipality after the events of the 16th and 17th of April. Firstly, was there a Ministry of National Defence under -- under a man named Milos Bogdanovic, who you've mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was this section, municipal section of the Ministry of Defence headed by Mr. Milos Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he later -- did he later -- was he later replaced by another man?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he replaced by?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was replaced by Mr. Bozo Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, I'd like to produce two documents to you now so that we can speed matters up, and I'd like you to quickly have a look at them. MR. DI FAZIO: For the purposes of Defence counsel, they are C74 and C68.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Todorovic, I do not wish to dwell too long on these documents. I only need to make one or two basic points from them. Would you please look at one document which is dated the 8th of June, 1992, and refers to the, I believe, appointment of Bozo Ninkovic. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document. I don't see exactly, is it the 8th of March or the 13th of March?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe the document should be dated the 8th of June. Can you see that at the top left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We won't quibble about the date. What about the signature at the bottom of the document? Is that apparently the signature of Dr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it resembles the signature of Mr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I know it's not clear but could you try and do your best? Look at paragraph 1. Does that apparently appoint Bozo Ninkovic as Secretary of the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now would you look at the other document? That is dated the 14th of June, I believe, and that should be a better copy. Again, is it apparently signed by Dr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it speaks for itself. It says Milos Bogdanovic is going to be relieved of that post in the Secretariat for the National Defence, does it not?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These two men, Bozo Ninkovic and Milos Bogdanovic, were they both on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos Bogdanovic was a member of the Crisis Staff while still being the head, while when he -- his function ended, he was replaced by Bozo Ninkovic, who then became also a member of the Crisis Staff. So they weren't on the Crisis Staff at the same time, the two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. One preceded the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For the record, just in question of my learned friend, it was page 74, line 12 and 13, he asks him: Milos Bogdanovic going to be relieved of the post in the Secretariat for National Defence? In fact, this document speaks for itself. It's the municipal secretariat. Just for the clarification, we are not speaking of the upper level of secretariat. It's municipal. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, thank you. I accept what Mr. Pantelic says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyway, these two men were members of the Crisis Staff but one followed the other?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one followed the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I produce the documents into evidence. Perhaps we could have them sequential so that C68 gets the first number and C74 gets the second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The one dated the 8th of June first. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, and the next number that's available and then the one dated the 14th of June, which is C74, gets the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be P86 ter and P86 for the decision dated 8 June, 1992, and it will be P87 and P87 ter for the document dated 14th of June, 1992. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, there is no doubt that people in Bosanski Samac were engaged in working after the 16th and 17th of April. It's been referred to as forced labour or work assignment. The title doesn't particularly interest me. What does interest me is this: Who was responsible for organising and conducting that work?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the organisation of the work assignment, the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence was the competent body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So both men that we have just been talking about, Bozo Ninkovic and Milos Bogdanovic, were heading up the body that dealt with this issue?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And both were members of the Crisis Staff. Did they from time to time report to the Crisis Staff about how that was going, the same way that you provided reports, Mr. Tadic provided reports, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- we've heard evidence that the Catholic church in Bosanski Samac was demolished and removed. Were people who engaged in work assignments or forced labour engaged in the removal of the remains of the church?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the removal of the remnants of the demolished church, the trucks were engaged, and machinery. Now, whether any of these people who were in detention, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about people in detention. I'm talking about people who were involved in forced labour or work assignments, people used to gather in front of the Spomen Dom building?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say that I didn't control or -- and I wasn't informed in detail, but as far as I know, these big concrete blocks of the demolished church were removed in big trucks and they were -- also used big machinery for loading on these trucks. And I'm not aware that the people who would be meeting in front of the pensioners' house centre, that they would be involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did people who performed work assignments or forced labour engage in digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, that was also the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I take it from your position in security and heading up the police and so on, it wasn't a matter that you concerned yourself with, the question of the work assignment and so on?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it's not in dispute in this case that at some point Odzak was taken over by Serb forces, after fighting. After that occurred, did Mr. Simo Zaric go there to carry out various duties?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man named Savo Popovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any role to play in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to Savo Popovic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he had a role.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the role of Mr. Simo Zaric in Odzak and what was the role of Mr. Savo Popovic in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Savo Popovic was the President of that civilian council, or whatever the name was, and Mr. Zaric was his assistant or deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had Savo Popovic ever been on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Crisis Staff in Samac?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was on the Crisis Staff, a member of the Crisis Staff in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he -- while he was working in Odzak on this assignment, whatever it was, was he still a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know how it was regulated, but I know that he would come to the Crisis Staff in Samac, asking for certain help, certain assistance, for the jobs that had to be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following the takeover of Odzak by Serb forces, did any people go there to perform forced labour or work assignment?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff ever deal with this issue in any way at all?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Savo Popovic would occasionally come. He would inform the members of the Crisis Staff that there are quite a number of demolished homes, that the agricultural works have to be performed, that the waterway has to be recovered, and that the consequences of war, they had to dwell on -- as a consequence of war, they had to do a lot of repair work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Did he need workers to help him do that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As there was only a small number of Serbs who were returning to their homes, their homes were mainly burned down and demolished, there weren't many able-bodied persons to work, and from Odzak, they requested help for this type of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I am interested in. Did Mr. Savo Popovic request help for carrying out the repair work following the battle in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that request made or conveyed to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff respond and find workers?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff usually responded positively, and referred Mr. Popovic to the Municipal Secretariat of National Defence, where he would be assigned a number of workers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this problem of cleaning up Odzak following the battle a fairly important matter that needed to be attended to, so far as you could gather from what you heard and saw?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say that it was an important matter, because the water pipes were ruptured, the telephone lines, and in order to organise life again there, this had to be repaired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this a matter that was being attended to, as far as you could tell, from the administration in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the administration of which Simo Zaric played a part, the administration in which he was working, along with Savo Popovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were specialists ever needed for the -- for this sort of cleaning-up activity, for example, electricians, plumbers and so on?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, they were essential, plumbers, electricians, and specialists for other areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this particular requirement for specialist workers made known to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Excuse me. Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: I do apologise, would Your Honours just bear with me for one moment longer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if women were engaged in working in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I've almost completed this topic, Mr. Todorovic. I may return to it briefly later on but, for the moment, I want to now turn to another topic and that is the question of seizure of goods and properties. MR. DI FAZIO: Again, would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to produce a document to you, Mr. Todorovic. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, Defence counsel will know of it as C25.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just acquaint yourself with that document, Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on this document, I don't think there is a very clear signature, but there is a stamp. Is that the Crisis Staff stamp?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It refers to Crisis Staffs of local communities taking over goods, material, equipment and other items confiscated or recovered from the zone of combat and keeping them in storage at Bosanac and Uniglas. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, were those places warehouses of goods, all sorts of goods, all types of goods?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, smaller quantity of goods was then stored there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I seek to tender that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the numbers, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It will be P88 ter for the B/C/S and P88. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honours, according to our position, we do have objections to the authenticity of this document. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, it's 1.45. Is this the time that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn and continue our proceedings on Monday at 9.00. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, perhaps on the issue that was raised by Mr. -- I believe that Ms. Reidy has a matter of some importance that she needs to raise with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: On the issue raised by Mr. Pantelic? MR. DI FAZIO: No, another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because I thought that -- I wanted to deal with that on Monday. Is there another matter? MR. DI FAZIO: It concerns the witness. So perhaps it's best if she speak to you about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Bench had requested information from the Prosecution on the witnesses to follow Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: That will be provided in writing. I think it's the easiest way to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: But the Bench is aware that one of those witnesses for whom a motion and protective measures will be sought, is going to be giving testimony via videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: It was our suggestion, in consultation with the registry, that this was okay, that that take place on the 19th of June. That would be Wednesday week. And that is one of the days that this gentleman is not attending dialysis treatment and is not in hospital and could do that. I think the Defence think that's okay. I don't want to put that in a motion if, for example, this witness is still on the stand by then or if that doesn't suit the Bench, but I would like to just take instruction from the Bench as to whether or not we should go ahead and put a videolink in place for the 19th of June, because it is something that requires, obviously, prior planning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is up to the Prosecution, how they line up their witnesses and also how you discuss with the people responsible for setting up videolink testimony. You can inform the Defence and discuss with them or put it in a confidential minute to them so that, if they have any objection, they can raise them, but I can't see any objections, because these are preparations -- these are arrangements which require time and consultation with other people who are not members of the Tribunal, necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. So do I take it that if we go ahead and set it up on the 19th as everybody on the logistical side has agreed it's possible, and we go ahead and do that, that should this witness still be in the process of cross-examination, we would take a break on the 19th of June to take this videolink testimony and then continue with this witness on the 19th? That's just really my concern I'd like to get instruction from the Bench on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What you want is that, once we start the videolink witness, we should, as much as possible, complete the evidence of that witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, given his hospital requirements, he would be done in one day but also, as I said, given the unpredictability of how long this current witness might take on the stand, it is possible he could still be finishing his cross on that date, although I would hope by Wednesday week he'll be finished. But we would nevertheless I hope interpose that videolink if all the arrangements are in place, notwithstanding the situation with this witness, if that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, I think you just put it in writing. It will be much clearer, and looking at the -- because Mr. Di Fazio knows how much longer he requires the witness in chief, for instance, and that could have repercussions on the time required for cross-examination. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll attempt to do my level best to try and stick to the timetable that I've indicated, but I'm optimistic that even in the worst-case scenario, we still wouldn't be going Wednesday week. So I don't think it will be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, please put your requirements for this videolink on paper so that the Defence are clear, and then they can make whatever submissions they want to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and continue our proceedings on Monday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: 1.50 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 10th day of June, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
